set1.q: What does five-year survival measure?
opts: Percent of patients alive five years from a point in their disease
Correct, and the starting point is some point in the course of the disease, which is why where that point falls matters.
Percent of patients cured after five years of treatment
Survival counts patients who are alive, not cured; a patient can be alive with disease at five years.
Percent of a population dying of the disease in five years
That describes disease-specific mortality, whose denominator is the population rather than patients.
Percent of patients whose disease returns within five years
That is the recurrence rate, which counts a return of disease after a disease-free interval.

set1.q: For which kind of cohort does a survival curve estimate survival?
opts: The actual cohort studied, exactly
The curve is an estimate for a hypothetical cohort, built from the interval probabilities.
Every patient with the disease worldwide
The curve is drawn from the patients studied, and generalizing beyond them needs further judgment.
A single patient followed to the end
One patient cannot yield a probability curve; it is built from a group followed over time.
A hypothetical cohort rather than an actual one
Correct: the curve is an estimate built from the interval probabilities, not the direct record of an actual group.

set1.q: What happens to a censored patient in a Kaplan-Meier analysis?
opts: Is counted as a death at that time
A censored patient has not died as far as is known; counting a death would lower the estimate falsely.
Leaves the number at risk without counting as a death
Correct: a censored patient is no longer followed, so the number at risk falls without a death being recorded.
Is counted as alive until the end of the study
That would keep the patient in the at-risk number even though follow-up has ended.
Is replaced by a newly enrolled patient
Patients are not replaced; the number at risk simply becomes smaller.

set1.q: What can bias do in a survival cohort study?
opts: Only exaggerate differences that exist
Bias can also obscure true differences, so its effect is not limited to exaggeration.
Only remove chance variation
Bias is systematic error and does not remove chance variation, which is reduced by design and analysis.
Falsely create or obscure real differences
Correct: bias can make a difference appear that is not there or hide one that is.
Improve the precision of every estimate
Bias distorts results in a systematic way and does not improve precision.

set1.q: A treated group has a hazard ratio of 0.4 compared with an untreated group. The treated group's risk is what proportion of the untreated group's?
opts: 40 percent
Correct: a hazard ratio below 1 is protective, and 0.4 means the treated group has 40 percent of the risk of the untreated group.
60 percent
Sixty percent is the reduction in risk, 1 minus 0.4, not the proportion of the untreated group's risk that remains.
250 percent
That would be the inverse, 1 divided by 0.4, which describes the untreated group's risk relative to the treated group's.
0.4 percent
This misplaces the decimal; 0.4 as a proportion is 40 percent.

set1.q: What is zero time in a prognosis study?
opts: The moment the last patient is enrolled
Zero time is a shared starting point in each patient's disease course, not the closing of enrollment.
The date on which the study is published
Publication has no bearing on where in the disease course each patient starts.
A shared point in the disease course
Correct: all cohort members should be identified at a similar point in the course of their disease.
The time at which the outcome occurs
The outcome comes at the end of follow-up; zero time is the starting point.

set1.q: Which is a question to ask when appraising a prognosis study?
opts: Were outcomes assessed objectively and blindly?

Correct, and the others are whether an inception cohort was assembled, whether entry criteria were objective, whether follow-up was adequate, whether the patients resemble yours and whether important prognostic factors were adjusted for.
Was the exposure assigned by the investigator?
That is a question for trials; a prognosis cohort observes patients rather than assigning them.
Were the participants free of the disease?
Prognosis studies enroll patients who have the disease, so healthy participants would signal a risk study.
Was the study limited to a single center?
A single center is a consideration for generalizability, but the appraisal asks whether the study patients resemble yours.

set1.q: Nine patients die after 3, 5, 6, 8, 11, 15, 20, 28 and 40 months. What is the median survival time?
opts: 15 months
That is the mean, 136 divided by 9 (15.1), which the longest survivors pull above the middle value.
11 months
Correct: the fifth of nine ordered values leaves four on each side, and the mean of 15.1 months is pulled up by the longest survivors.
8 months
That is the fourth value; with nine values the middle is the fifth.
20 months
That is the seventh value; with nine ordered values the middle one is the fifth.

set1.q: What does a clinical prediction rule estimate?
opts: The prevalence of disease in a community
Prevalence is measured by counting cases in a population; a prediction rule estimates an outcome for an individual patient.
Outcome probability from patient characteristics
Correct, using a set of characteristics rather than one finding, which predicts outcome better than any single data point.
The sensitivity of a test in a new setting
Test properties are measured against a gold standard; a prediction rule estimates the chance of an outcome.
The best treatment from a list of drugs
A prediction rule estimates how likely an outcome is, and choosing a treatment is a separate decision.

set1.io: Discuss the clinical course and natural history of disease
set1.q: As new treatments arise, what are they compared with?
opts: The outcome in healthy people
Healthy people do not have the disease, so their outcome cannot show what a treatment changes; the comparison is the untreated course.
The cost of the older treatment
Cost may matter to decisions, but the comparison that establishes benefit is against the natural, untreated outcome of the disease.
The opinion of the treating clinician
Opinion is not a measured outcome; a new treatment is judged against the natural, untreated outcome of the disease.
The natural, untreated outcome of disease
Correct, because the untreated course is the baseline that shows whether a new treatment changes what would otherwise happen.

set1.q: Why is the generalizability of a prognosis study often limited?
opts: Its follow-up is always too short
Follow-up may be adequate; the limit arises from who the study patients are.
Its outcomes cannot be measured
Outcomes such as survival can be measured; the limit concerns who was studied.
Its patients may not represent others
Correct: they may also not represent an individual patient, so how similar they are to yours must be judged.
Its patients were always randomized
Randomization deals with bias between groups but does not make the patients representative of other populations.

set1.q: How does the proportion of dropouts affect the potential for bias?
opts: Potential for bias falls as dropouts increase
The opposite is true; with more dropouts, the patients remaining are more likely to differ from those who left.
Potential for bias rises as dropouts increase
Correct: the key question is whether dropouts are similar to those who stay in the study.
Dropouts have no effect on bias
Dropouts can remove patients who differ from those who stay, which biases the outcome.
Dropouts only matter when they recover
Death, recovery and disability all cause dropout, and any of them can bias the results.

set1.io: Discuss the clinical course and natural history of disease
set1.q: Why does the severity of a disease matter?
opts: It sets priorities for health services
Correct: knowing how severe the natural course is tells planners where clinical services and public health programs are most needed.
It fixes how many risk factors a patient has
Risk factors are features that raise the chance of disease and do not follow from severity; severity's role is in setting priorities for services.
It fixes the cost of every treatment
Cost does not follow from severity; the value of measuring severity is that it establishes priorities for services.
It removes the need to study outcomes
Severity is itself established by studying outcomes, using measures such as death, disability and discomfort.

set1.q: The chances of surviving three successive intervals are 90, 80 and 50 percent. What is the probability of surviving all three?
opts: 36 percent
Correct: the cumulative probability is the product, 0.90 times 0.80 times 0.50, which is 0.36.
73 percent
This averages the three probabilities; survival to a later point is the product of the interval probabilities, not their mean.
50 percent
This is the probability for the last interval alone and ignores the two intervals that came before it.
90 percent
This is the probability for the first interval alone and ignores the two later intervals.

set1.q: Where on a survival curve is the estimate most precise?
opts: Late on, at the right side
Fewer participants remain late in follow-up, so the estimate there is less precise.
Early on, at the left side
Correct: more of the population remains under observation early on, so the estimate is based on a larger group.
Wherever the curve plateaus
A plateau reflects few participants still followed and so is less reliable, not more.
Equally at every point along the curve
Precision falls as the number of participants still followed falls, so it differs along the curve.

set1.q: What is prognosis?
opts: The identification of a disease from its findings
That is diagnosis, which names the disease; prognosis begins after it is named and predicts how the disease will unfold.
The chance a healthy person develops a disease
That is risk, which concerns who becomes ill; prognosis concerns what happens to people who already have the disease.
The cause of a disease in one patient
Cause is a question of etiology; prognosis predicts the future course of the disease, whatever its cause.
A prediction of the course of a disease
Correct, and it is what a clinician tries to estimate once a diagnosis is made, in terms such as survival, complications or disability.

set1.q: What is migration bias?
opts: Groups differ in disease course at entry
That is susceptibility bias, which arises from how the groups were assembled.
One group has its outcomes detected more often
That is measurement bias, which arises from how the outcome is classified.
Patients drop out of the study or change groups
Correct: the reasons include death, recovery and disability.
Patients are chosen for convenience
That is a source of selection bias arising when the cohort is assembled rather than during follow-up.

set1.io: Discuss the clinical course and natural history of disease
set1.q: Which stage comes first in the clinical course of disease?
opts: Biologic onset
Correct: the sequence runs from biologic onset through evident pathology, signs and symptoms, care sought, diagnosis and treatment to outcome.
Signs and symptoms present
Symptoms appear only after the disease has begun and pathology has become evident.
Medical care sought
The patient seeks care after signs and symptoms appear, well after biologic onset.
Diagnosis given
Diagnosis follows the patient seeking medical care, so it cannot be the first stage.

set1.io: Discuss the clinical course and natural history of disease
set1.q: When in the course of disease can screening find it?
opts: Before signs and symptoms appear
Correct, during the preclinical phase, which is what allows screening to detect disease at an earlier point.
Only after a diagnosis is given
Screening exists to find disease before diagnosis, so it applies before a diagnosis is given.
Only once medical care is sought
By the time the patient seeks care the disease has usually produced signs and symptoms, past the point where screening adds anything.
After the outcome has occurred
The outcome ends the clinical course, so nothing remains to be detected or treated.

set1.io: Discuss the clinical course and natural history of disease
set1.q: What characterizes the preclinical phase of a disease?
opts: Symptoms are present but no diagnosis exists
Once signs and symptoms appear, the disease has entered the clinical phase.
Treatment has begun but symptoms remain
Treatment occurs in the clinical phase, after diagnosis, so it cannot mark the preclinical phase.
The outcome has already occurred
The outcome is the end point of the clinical course, so it comes long after the preclinical phase.
Disease is present but symptoms have not appeared
Correct, and this is the window in which screening can find disease, before signs and symptoms bring the patient to care.

set1.q: Which statement about prognosis is true?
opts: It is what occurs without any intervention
That describes the natural history of disease; prognosis is the predicted course, which treatment can improve.
It is fixed at the moment of biologic onset
The course is not fixed at onset; treatment, earlier detection and other factors can shift where a patient ends up.
It cannot be expressed in numbers
Prognosis is routinely expressed quantitatively through rates such as five-year survival, remission and recurrence.
It can often be improved by clinical intervention
Correct, whereas natural history is what occurs without intervention, which is the contrast that gives prognosis its clinical value.

set1.q: Five-year survival is 54 percent in people with a disease and 90 percent expected in people of the same age without it. What is the relative survival?
opts: 36 percent
That is the difference between the two figures; relative survival is their ratio.
167 percent
That inverts the ratio, 0.90 divided by 0.54; the observed survival goes on top.
72 percent
That averages the two figures; relative survival divides observed by expected.
60 percent
Correct: observed survival divided by expected survival is 0.54 divided by 0.90, which is 0.60.

set1.q: Why can five-year survival not evaluate a therapy introduced two years ago?
opts: Newer therapies never improve survival
New therapies can improve survival; the problem is that not enough time has passed to measure five-year outcomes.
No one has yet been followed for five years
Correct: patients treated with a therapy introduced within the past five years, or with a disease duration under five years, cannot be evaluated.
Five-year survival applies only to screening
Five-year survival is a general outcome measure, though screening creates one of its biases.
The natural history has been changed
A changed natural history is what treatment aims for; the obstacle here is only insufficient follow-up time.

set1.io: Compare and contrast risk and prognostic factors
set1.q: Which factor appears both as a risk factor for infarction and as a poor prognostic factor after it?
opts: Anterior infarction
This is a poor prognostic factor that can only be present once an infarction has occurred, so it cannot be a risk factor for it.
Ventricular arrhythmia
It is a poor prognostic factor after infarction rather than a factor that leads a healthy person to have one.
Cigarette smoking
Correct: smoking raises the chance of infarction and also worsens the outlook after one, as does increasing age.
Hypotension
Hypotension is a poor prognostic factor; the blood pressure abnormality on the risk list is hypertension.

set1.io: Discuss the clinical course and natural history of disease
set1.q: Which of these is one of the five Ds used to describe the outcomes of disease?
opts: Dissatisfaction
Correct: the five Ds are death, disease, discomfort, disability and dissatisfaction.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is a stage in the clinical course rather than one of the five Ds; the Ds are death, disease, discomfort, disability and dissatisfaction.
Deterioration
Deterioration is not on the list, which consists of death, disease, discomfort, disability and dissatisfaction.
Dependency
Dependency is not on the list, which consists of death, disease, discomfort, disability and dissatisfaction.

set1.q: How can prognosis be expressed quantitatively?
opts: As the number of risk factors present
Counting risk factors describes who is likely to become ill, not the course of an established disease, which is what prognosis quantifies.
As the sensitivity of the test used
Sensitivity describes how well a test detects disease; prognosis is quantified by how often outcomes occur among patients with the disease.
As a rate, such as five-year survival
Correct, and other examples are the case-fatality, response, remission and recurrence rates, each stating how often an outcome occurs.
As the cost of the treatment given
Cost says nothing about what happens to patients; prognosis is quantified with outcome rates such as survival and remission.

set1.io: Discuss the clinical course and natural history of disease
set1.q: With what should the outcome of a new treatment be compared?
opts: The course in people without the disease
Healthy people do not have the disease, so their course is no benchmark for what a treatment achieves.
The natural, untreated course of the disease
Correct, because only against the untreated outcome can a treatment's effect on prognosis be judged.
The cost of the most expensive alternative
Cost is a separate consideration; effect is judged against the outcome without treatment.
The course in patients who were cured
Selecting only cured patients would bias the comparison; the benchmark is the natural course of the disease.

set1.q: What is an advantage of median survival time?
opts: It uses every death in the cohort
A mean uses every value, whereas the median depends on the middle of the distribution.
It can be found before all have died
Correct: it is also less affected by extreme values, so a few very long or short survivors do not move it much.
It adjusts for the age of the patients
Age adjustment is what relative survival does, comparing observed with expected survival.
It requires no follow-up of patients
Patients still have to be followed until half of them have died.

set1.q: Besides biologic outcomes, what should outcome measurement include?
opts: Only the date of death
Death is one outcome, but the full range of manifestations should be included, including quality of life.
Only laboratory values
Laboratory values are biologic measures; clinical outcomes and quality of life should be considered alongside them.
Clinical outcomes and quality of life
Correct: the full range of manifestations should be covered, biological and clinical, together with quality of life.
Only outcomes the patient can hide
Outcomes should be objectively assessed and cover the full range of manifestations, not a subset chosen by concealment.

set1.q: What does survival analysis calculate when people enter at various times?
opts: The prevalence at a single moment
Prevalence is a snapshot at one time and does not account for how long each person was followed.
The sensitivity of the outcome measure
Sensitivity describes test accuracy, not the follow-up time contributed by each person.
The random error of each measurement
Random error is estimated statistically; the follow-up contributed by each person is measured in person-years.
The person-years each person contributes
Correct: people can be added at different points in their disease and each contributes the time they are followed.

set2.q: How can the natural history of a disease be changed to improve prognosis?
opts: Through clinical intervention
Correct, and the further aim is to detect disease at an earlier point so that treatment is as effective as it can be.
Through longer observation alone
Watching a disease without acting describes its natural history rather than changing it; only an intervention can alter the course.
Through more precise measurement
Better measurement improves how outcomes are described but does nothing to change what happens to the patient.
Through larger study cohorts
A larger cohort makes an estimate more precise; it does not change the disease course, which requires an intervention.

set2.q: Of 240 people who have a disease, 18 die of it. What is the case-fatality ratio?
opts: 92.5 percent
That is the proportion who survived, 222 of 240; the case-fatality ratio counts those who die.
13.3 percent
That inverts the fraction, 240 divided by 18 (13.3), rather than dividing deaths by the number with the disease.
0.75 percent
This misplaces the decimal; 18 divided by 240 is 0.075, or 7.5 percent.
7.5 percent
Correct: 18 deaths divided by 240 people with the disease is 0.075.

set2.q: In the Kaplan-Meier method, what starts a new interval?
opts: The end of each calendar year
Fixed intervals such as death at one year are what the method replaces with intervals set by each death.
The exact time each death occurs
Correct, and this is what generates the stepwise curve, in place of pre-determined intervals such as death at 1 year.
The enrollment of each new patient
Enrollment adds patients to the cohort but does not start an interval; each death does.
Every scheduled follow-up visit
Visits do not define the intervals; the exact time of each death does.

set2.q: Why are several prognostic factors used together?
opts: Each factor alone predicts outcome perfectly
No single data point predicts outcome perfectly, which is exactly why combining several factors is preferred.
Together they remove the need to follow patients
Outcomes still have to be observed to build and test any prediction; combining factors only sharpens the estimate.
Together they cancel every source of bias
Combining factors improves prediction but does not cancel bias, which is handled by design and analysis.
Together they predict outcome better than one finding
Correct, and clinical prediction rules exploit this by combining a set of patient characteristics into one estimate.

set2.q: What is the median survival time?
opts: The average of everyone's survival time
That is the mean, which extreme values pull up or down, unlike the median.
The time until the last patient dies
That is the longest survival, which one unusual patient can determine, unlike the median.
The time half the population survives
Correct, and it can be read from the curve at the point where survival crosses 50 percent.
The survival expected without the disease
That is the expected survival used in relative survival, not the median.

set2.q: Which finding worsens prognosis after an acute myocardial infarction?
opts: Younger age
Increasing age, not younger age, is the poor prognostic factor; younger patients tend to fare better.
Congestive heart failure
Correct, one of the poor prognostic factors, alongside ventricular arrhythmia, anterior infarction, hypotension and increasing age.
Normal blood pressure
Hypotension is the blood pressure finding that marks a poor prognosis, not a normal pressure.
Never having smoked
Cigarette smoking is the factor that is unfavorable, so never having smoked does not worsen the outlook.

set2.q: The hazard ratio from a Cox analysis is interpreted like which measure?
opts: Relative risk (risk ratio)
Correct: a hazard ratio above 1 means more risk of the outcome than the comparison group, and below 1 means less.
Sensitivity
Sensitivity is the probability that a person with disease tests positive, a measure of test accuracy.
Prevalence
Prevalence is the proportion of a population with a condition at one time and is not a ratio of risks.
Positive predictive value
Predictive value describes what a positive test result means, unlike a ratio comparing risk between two groups.

set2.q: What is the aim of detecting a disease at an earlier point?
opts: To lengthen the preclinical phase
The aim is not to change how long the disease exists before symptoms; it is to treat while treatment works best.
To maximize the effectiveness of treatment
Correct, though earlier detection helps only if treatment given sooner actually changes the outcome, which is not automatic.
To avoid ever needing follow-up
Follow-up remains necessary to measure outcomes; earlier detection only aims to make the treatment given more effective.
To raise the reported survival rate
Earlier detection can inflate a survival rate without helping anyone; the true aim is to improve what treatment achieves.

set2.q: What is the denominator of disease-specific mortality?
opts: Patients with the disease
That is the denominator of case fatality, which is why case fatality measures severity among the sick.
Deaths from all causes
That is the denominator of proportionate mortality, a proportion of deaths rather than a rate in a population.
Patients who received treatment
Disease-specific mortality is not limited to treated patients; it is measured against the entire population.
The whole population
Correct: it is the number of people per 10,000 or 100,000 population dying of the disease, unlike case fatality, which uses patients.

set2.q: What is susceptibility bias?
opts: Patients drop out or change groups
That is migration bias, which arises during follow-up rather than in how the groups were assembled.
The assembled groups differ in ways that affect outcome
Correct: for example the groups may be at different points in the disease course, have other concurrent disease, or have had prior treatment.
One group's outcomes are more likely to be detected
That is measurement bias, which arises from how the outcome is classified and detected.
Results apply only to a narrow population
That concerns generalizability, which is limited when study patients are not representative of other populations.

set2.q: For which kind of disease is the case-fatality ratio most useful?
opts: Chronic disease with survival of decades
When deaths occur years later, a ratio taken soon after diagnosis would miss them, so survival measures are used instead.
Any disease that is very common
How common a disease is does not decide it; the ratio suits acute disease in which death follows diagnosis quickly.
Acute disease where death follows quickly
Correct: it suits acute, short-term disease where death occurs shortly after diagnosis, so the deaths can be counted without long follow-up.
Disease that never causes death
With no deaths the ratio would always be zero and would say nothing about the disease's course.

set2.q: Which is a source of selection bias in a cohort?
opts: Convenience or volunteer samples
Correct, along with declines from among those selected and dropouts.
Blinded outcome assessment
Blinding is a way to minimize measurement bias, not a source of selection bias.
Strict criteria for the outcome
Strict criteria for judging the outcome help reduce measurement bias rather than cause selection bias.
Random assignment of patients
Randomization is a method to control selection bias, not a source of it.

set2.q: When is an inception cohort assembled?
opts: After treatment has been completed
By then the course has been altered, so patients would no longer share a similar starting point.
When the disease first becomes apparent
Correct: the aim is to assemble it as early as possible and as uniformly as possible.
At the time of the outcome event
Assembling patients at the outcome would ignore the disease course that led to it.
Once symptoms have peaked in severity
Patients reach their peak at different times, so this would not give a uniform starting point.

set2.io: Compare and contrast risk and prognostic factors
set2.q: Who takes part in a risk study?
opts: People already sick
Sick participants are the subjects of prognosis studies, which follow what happens after the disease appears.
People in remission
Remission is an outcome of disease, so it belongs to prognosis studies rather than risk studies.
People who have died
Death is an outcome studied in prognosis, in participants who were sick, rather than the population of a risk study.
Healthy people
Correct, because the question is who goes on to develop the disease, and the outcome of interest is diagnosis.

set2.q: A cancer begins in 2001. Screening finds it in 2005, but without screening it would have been diagnosed in 2009. Death occurs in 2011 either way. By how many years does survival from diagnosis appear longer with screening?
opts: Six years
Six years is the survival from diagnosis in the screened patient alone, not the difference between the two.
Four years
Correct: survival from diagnosis is 6 years with screening (2005 to 2011) against 2 without (2009 to 2011), yet death did not come any later.
Two years
Two years is the survival from diagnosis without screening; the difference from six years is four.
Ten years
Ten years is the time from biologic onset to death in the unscreened patient, not the extra survival from diagnosis.

set2.q: What is the case-fatality rate?
opts: Percent of patients with a disease who die of it
Correct, and because its denominator is patients with the disease it measures the severity of the disease itself.
Deaths from a disease per 100,000 population
That is disease-specific mortality, whose denominator is the whole population rather than the patients.
Percent of patients who improve after treatment
That is the response rate, which counts patients showing some evidence of improvement following an intervention.
Percent of patients whose disease is undetectable
That is the remission rate, which counts patients entering a phase in which disease is no longer detectable.

set2.q: What do near-identical five-year survival rates fail to show?
opts: When the deaths occur
Correct: conditions such as a dissecting aneurysm, lung cancer and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis can share one five-year rate while their survival curves differ greatly.
How many patients were studied
The sample size is reported separately from the rate and is not what the rate conceals.
Which patients had the disease
The rate is calculated for patients who have the disease; what it conceals is when the deaths happen.
Whether the disease exists
The rate presumes the disease exists; it does not describe the timing of deaths within the five years.

set2.q: What is a use of Cox proportional hazards regression?
opts: Studying an exposure's effect after adjusting for confounders
Correct: it resembles Kaplan-Meier but can adjust for confounders and take account of several predictors at once.
Drawing a curve from the exact time of each death
That is the Kaplan-Meier method, which Cox regression resembles but extends.
Calculating the person-years contributed by each patient
Person-years come from follow-up time; Cox regression estimates the effect of exposures on the outcome.
Finding the time at which half the group has died
That is the median survival time, which a Cox regression is not designed to give.

set2.io: Compare and contrast risk and prognostic factors
set2.q: What is true of a risk factor's effect on prognosis?
opts: It always worsens prognosis
Not so; a factor that raises the chance of getting a disease need not change how patients fare once they have it.
It always improves prognosis
Nothing guarantees an improvement; risk factors and prognostic factors answer different questions and can differ.
It need not worsen prognosis
Correct: risk factors do not necessarily represent a poorer prognosis, so being at risk of a disease and faring badly with it are separate questions.
It sets the case-fatality rate
The case-fatality rate is the percent of patients with a disease who die of it, and depends on prognostic factors and treatment.

set2.io: Compare and contrast risk and prognostic factors
set2.q: What is the outcome of interest in a risk study?
opts: Death or disability
Death, complications and disability are outcomes of prognosis studies, measured in participants who are already sick.
Diagnosis of the disease
Correct: the healthy participants are followed to see who is diagnosed, which is why rates are low and diagnosis is rare.
Response to treatment
Response is an outcome measured in patients receiving an intervention, which is a feature of prognosis studies.
Recurrence after remission
Recurrence can occur only in people who have already had the disease, which makes it a prognosis outcome.

set2.q: Of 250 patients diagnosed with a cancer, 150 are alive five years later and none were lost to follow-up. What is the five-year survival rate?
opts: 40 percent
That is the percent who died, 100 of 250; survival counts those still alive at five years.
25 percent
This would mean only about 62 of the 250 patients survived, not the 150 stated.
15 percent
This would mean only about 38 of the 250 patients were alive, whereas 150 were.
60 percent
Correct: 150 divided by 250 is 0.60, and with no one lost to follow-up every patient is accounted for.

set2.q: Why can five-year survival rise after screening without anyone living longer?
opts: Screening cures the disease in every patient
If screening cured everyone, patients would live longer in reality; the artifact arises when treatment does not change the natural history.
Screening lowers the number of people tested
The artifact does not come from the number tested but from starting the survival clock earlier.
Screening shortens the period of follow-up
Follow-up is not shortened; survival is counted from an earlier diagnosis to an unchanged date of death.
Diagnosis moves earlier while death does not
Correct: patients live longer only with a diagnosis, so the clock starts sooner while death occurs at a similar point.

set2.q: Which poor prognostic factor after myocardial infarction is not a risk factor for developing coronary disease?
opts: Physical inactivity
Inactivity is a risk factor for developing coronary disease, so it fails the condition of the question.
Increased cholesterol on the lipid panel
Increased low-density lipoprotein with decreased high-density lipoprotein is a risk factor for developing coronary disease.
Ventricular arrhythmia
Correct, because it arises after the infarction and predicts a worse outcome, but it is not something that leads a healthy person into coronary disease.
Hypertension
Hypertension is a risk factor for developing coronary disease; hypotension is the pressure finding that marks a poor prognosis after infarction.

set2.io: Discuss the clinical course and natural history of disease
set2.q: What is the natural history of a disease?
opts: What occurs without intervention
Correct, which is why it serves as the untreated benchmark against which new treatments are compared.
What occurs once treatment begins
That describes the treated course, which is what gets compared against the natural history.
The pattern of spread through a community
Spread through a community is an epidemiologic pattern; natural history follows the disease within an individual.
The history the patient reports
The history taken from a patient is part of the clinical encounter, not the untreated course of the disease.

set2.q: Which pair of endpoints can be used to describe prognosis?
opts: Screening or diagnosis
Screening and diagnosis are steps in detecting disease, not outcomes of it; the endpoints of prognosis are results such as cure or death.
Incidence or prevalence
These are measures of how much disease occurs in a population, not the outcomes that follow once a person has the disease.
Sensitivity or specificity
These describe the accuracy of a test; prognosis uses outcome endpoints, such as cure or death.
Cure or death
Correct, and these sit alongside the rates used to describe outcomes, such as five-year survival and remission.

set2.q: Which is a way to minimize measurement bias?
opts: Matching the groups on age
Matching is a method for controlling selection bias rather than measurement bias.
Blinding those who assess the outcome
Correct, together with strict criteria for whether the outcome occurred and equal effort to discover outcomes in all groups.
Restricting the sample to one clinic
Restriction controls selection bias by narrowing who is enrolled, not how the outcome is detected.
Stratifying the analysis by sex
Stratification is a method for controlling selection bias in the analysis and does not affect how outcomes are detected.

set2.q: What kind of factors do prognosis studies look for?
opts: Factors that cause the disease to begin
Factors that cause disease onset are risk factors, studied in healthy people rather than in patients.
Factors that raise the chance of diagnosis
Predicting diagnosis is the concern of risk studies; prognosis studies look at what happens after the diagnosis.
Factors that protect or promote progression
Correct, and these can differ from the factors that raise the chance of getting the disease in the first place.
Factors that change a test's sensitivity
Test sensitivity is a property of diagnostic accuracy; prognosis studies examine outcomes in sick participants.

set2.q: What does adjustment for important prognostic factors address in a prognosis study?
opts: Whether the outcome was measured blindly
Blinded assessment of the outcome is a separate appraisal question and addresses measurement bias.
Whether patients were followed long enough
Adequacy of follow-up is its own appraisal question, unrelated to adjusting for prognostic factors.
Whether other factors explain the outcome
Correct: groups can differ in prognosis because of some other factor rather than the one under study, and adjustment accounts for that.
Whether the entry criteria were objective
Objective, reasonable entry criteria are a separate appraisal question about how the cohort was assembled.

set2.q: Which method of controlling selection bias also handles factors nobody measured?
opts: Matching
Matching balances only the factors chosen for matching and leaves unmeasured factors uncontrolled.
Restriction
Restriction limits enrollment on selected characteristics, so it does nothing about factors nobody measured.
Randomization
Correct: it is the only method of dealing with differences between groups whose benefits are not limited to the factors selected for consideration.
Stratification
Stratification separates patients by chosen factors and so cannot address the ones that were never measured.

set2.q: What do prognostic factors identify?
opts: Patients with the same disease but different prognoses
Correct, which is what makes them useful: they separate patients who share a diagnosis into groups that fare differently.
Healthy people who will develop the disease
That is the job of risk factors, which predict who becomes ill rather than how ill patients fare.
Patients with different diseases and equal prognoses
Prognostic factors work within one disease, separating patients who have it into better and worse outcomes.
Tests that confirm a diagnosis
Confirming a diagnosis is the job of diagnostic tests; prognostic factors predict the outcome once the disease is known.
